title: Polylogarithmic dynamic maximal matching against adaptive updates
formal:
Does there exist a uniform randomized algorithm that explicitly maintains a maximal matching in a fully dynamic \(n\)-vertex simple graph against an adaptive adversary, with polylogarithmic expected amortized update time? More precisely, are there an algorithm and constants \(C,c>0\) such that, for every \(n\ge2\), every horizon \(T\ge1\), and every valid adaptive update strategy, the algorithm is always correct and its expected total update work is at most
\[C T(\log_2(n+2))^c,\]
after initialization in at most \(C n(\log_2(n+2))^c\) expected time? The graph starts empty and each update inserts or deletes one edge. The model and adversary are defined below. A deterministic algorithm is permitted as a special case.

This card selects the polylogarithmic question expressly included in the 2022 source. Its earlier sublinear-time question has since received positive answers; that weaker threshold is retained as dated progress rather than presented as open.
why: Maximal matching is a basic dynamic graph primitive whose current answer can influence the next change to the graph. This problem asks whether the cost of responding to that feedback can be reduced to a polylogarithm. It would clarify a major difference between algorithms that assume an independently chosen update sequence and algorithms whose guarantees survive interaction.

sentences: A graph changes through edge insertions and deletions while an explicit maximal matching must remain available.
The next change may depend on the matching the algorithm has just produced.
The question asks for an always-correct algorithm with polylogarithmic expected amortized update time against this adaptive feedback.
Deterministic algorithms now achieve a square-root-scale amortized bound, resolving the older sublinear threshold.
The much stronger polylogarithmic target remains distinct from constant-time results for update sequences fixed independently of the algorithm.

definitions:
The fixed vertex set is \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). The graph is undirected, loopless and simple, with no sparsity, degree or bipartiteness promise. An insertion gives two distinct vertex labels whose edge is currently absent; a deletion specifies a currently present edge. Both kinds may occur in any order, and the next update is unavailable until the current one is finished.

A matching \(M\subseteq E\) has no two edges sharing an endpoint. It is maximal if no edge of \(E\setminus M\) can be added while preserving this condition; equivalently, every edge of the graph has at least one endpoint incident to \(M\). The requirement is inclusion-wise maximality after every update. No maximum-cardinality optimality requirement is imposed.

Explicit maintenance means retaining an array \(\mathrm{mate}[1..n]\) with value zero for an unmatched vertex and value \(v\) at \(u\) when \(\{u,v\}\in M\). Array changes are charged to update time; reading one mate entry takes constant time. The whole matching need not be printed after each update.

Use a word-RAM with words of \(w=\lceil c_w\log_2(n+2)\rceil\) bits for a fixed constant \(c_w\) chosen with the algorithm, polynomially many addressable words of persistent memory, and unit-cost word reads, writes, comparisons, branches, Boolean operations, shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), and integer quotient/remainder by a nonzero word. Each independent uniform random word also costs one operation. All preprocessing, memory management and changes to the maintained matching are charged. The algorithm has one finite program for all \(n\), with no graph-dependent advice or uncharged table depending on the input. Its memory bound and word-size constant are fixed independently of the update horizon.

Before selecting update \(t+1\), the adversary may inspect the complete current matching, all previous updates and all observed update runtimes. It has unbounded computation and may use its own independent randomness. It does not see hidden algorithm state, past unexposed random choices or future random bits. Correctness and expected cost must hold for every such adaptive strategy, with the horizon \(T\) fixed before the experiment. The expectation includes randomness of both parties. Allowing the adversary to inspect the matching is an observation convention, not a requirement to print the array at every step.

Always correct means that every completed update returns a valid maximal matching, and every finite valid adaptive experiment terminates with probability one. Randomness may affect running time and which maximal matching is chosen, but may never permit an incorrect answer. This is a Las Vegas guarantee. The total-time inequality is amortized: a single update may cost more than a polylogarithm, provided every finite prefix obeys the stated expected total bound. All constants are independent of \(n,T\), the graph and the adversary.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of existence or nonexistence of an algorithm with these guarantees. A positive answer must maintain an explicit maximal matching for all valid adaptive insertion/deletion sequences, with the stated uniformity, always-correct behavior and expected prefix-total bounds. A bound only against an oblivious adversary, a maintained estimate of maximum matching size, or a matching that is approximately maximum but not maximal is insufficient. A merely sublinear polynomial update bound does not reach the polylogarithmic target. A negative answer must rule out randomized algorithms in this model, not just one deterministic implementation.

context_blocks.text: The original problem paragraph asks several related questions. This review takes its explicit polylogarithmic target and fixes the permissive expected-amortized, always-correct randomized setting against an adversary observing the matching. It does not combine the separate lower-bound question into the answer criterion.

The 2026 paper reports earlier oblivious-adversary algorithms with constant amortized update time and polylogarithmic worst-case update time. Those guarantees assume that the update sequence cannot adapt to the maintained matching.

Bernstein, Bhattacharya, Kiss and Saranurak’s STOC 2025 results, summarized in the 2026 introduction, achieve \(\widetilde O(n^{3/4})\) randomized adaptive update time and \(\widetilde O(n^{8/9})\) deterministic update time, both amortized. Thus the source’s basic sublinear threshold is no longer the open target.

Chuzhoy, Khanna and Song’s Theorem 1.1 gives a deterministic fully dynamic algorithm with amortized update time \(n^{1/2+o(1)}\). This also tolerates adaptive updates, but its guarantee does not supply polylogarithmic update time. Here \(\widetilde O\) suppresses polylogarithmic factors, and \(o(1)\) in the exponent tends to zero as \(n\) grows.
